summary: The Linux Foundation’s umbrella for open-source networking: OpenDaylight, ONAP, FD.io, Nephio, Anuket and newer projects for telecom and cloud networks, sharing one budget and a technical advisory council.
intro: LF Networking (LFN) is part of the non-profit Linux Foundation. It was formed in January 2018 by combining six networking projects that the Linux Foundation already hosted, ONAP, OPNFV, OpenDaylight, FD.io, PNDA and SNAS, with 83 member organisations at the start. Joining was voluntary, and each project kept its own technical steering committee, release roadmap and website, while staff and money were pooled under one governing board. The governing board, made up of representatives of paying members, oversees finance, budgets and strategy, and a Technical Advisory Council (TAC) is responsible for communication and collaboration between the projects.

Most of its work serves telecom operators and their suppliers. In October 2026 the LFN wiki listed five graduated projects: OpenDaylight, an SDN controller; ONAP, for orchestrating network services; FD.io, home of the VPP software data plane; Nephio, Kubernetes-based automation for network functions; and Anuket, reference specifications for telecom clouds. Incubating were the 5G Super Blueprint, L3AF, a project for eBPF kernel functions, and the O-RAN Software Community; CNTi and Paraglider, a control plane for tenant networking on public clouds, were in the sandbox, and Duranta, Essedum, StratoWeave and OpenAN were candidates. Nine projects had been archived or merged, including Tungsten Fabric, the SDN platform Juniper open-sourced in 2013 as OpenContrail.

For someone choosing a technology, an LFN badge says the project is run in the open at the Linux Foundation, and the stage says how far it has come: graduated projects have shown a documented release process, a diverse community and the ability to run themselves, and they get a voting seat on the TAC. The badge doesn’t promise that a project is still widely used, and archiving is a real risk to watch: a project can be archived after 12 months without significant commits, and Tungsten Fabric, PNDA and SNAS, three of the first seven, are already archived.

sections.title: The lifecycle, and where projects sit
sections.intro: States and criteria are from the LFN lifecycle guidelines; project states are from the LFN wiki overview in October 2026.

items.name: Candidate
items.text: Projects asking to join, which can enter at any state if they already meet Linux Foundation best practices. To move into the sandbox, a candidate completes its formation as a Linux Foundation project and presents to the TAC. Duranta, CU/DU and UE software for end-to-end 5G testing built with the OpenAirInterface Software Alliance, Essedum, StratoWeave and OpenAN were candidates.

items.name: Sandbox
items.text: The entry state for early projects that still need to build a community, governance and roadmap; LFN staff give them hands-on help. CNTi, the Cloud Native Telecom Initiative, and Paraglider were here.

items.name: Incubation
items.text: Projects that have shown open-source best practices, a varied contributor base and open governance, and are moving towards managing themselves: the 5G Super Blueprint, L3AF and the O-RAN Software Community.

items.name: Graduated
items.text: Mature projects with a documented release process followed consistently, diversity, and readiness to manage themselves. Each gets a voting representative on the TAC. OpenDaylight, ONAP, FD.io, Nephio and Anuket were graduated.

items.name: Maintenance / LTS
items.text: For projects that have reached a stable, feature-complete state and focus on bug fixes, security updates and long-term support rather than new features; staff help is reduced to what is needed.

items.name: Archived
items.text: A project can be archived when it has had no significant commits in the previous 12 months, or when its steering committee asks; its work is kept read-only. OPNFV and CNTT were merged into Anuket in January 2021; Tungsten Fabric, PNDA, SNAS, OpenSwitch (OPX), EMCO, XGVela and ODIM were archived.

story: The Linux Foundation hosted several networking projects side by side by 2017, each with its own board, budget and membership: OpenDaylight, the SDN controller launched in 2013; FD.io, a fast software data plane; OPNFV, an integration platform for network functions virtualisation; ONAP, for orchestrating network services; and the smaller PNDA and SNAS analytics projects. Operators and vendors were paying into several of them at once.

In January 2018 the six were combined into the LF Networking Fund, with 83 members, a single governing board, shared staff and a TAC, while each project kept its charter and release schedule. In March 2018 Juniper’s OpenContrail completed its move to the Linux Foundation as Tungsten Fabric and joined LFN, the first project to go through its induction process. In January 2021 OPNFV and the CNTT specification effort merged into Anuket.

Later the umbrella moved towards cloud-native and Kubernetes-based networking. Nephio, for automating network functions with Kubernetes, has since graduated, and newer arrivals include L3AF, a project for eBPF kernel functions, and Paraglider for tenant networking on public clouds. Older projects such as Tungsten Fabric and PNDA were archived.

choices.why: Sharing staff, events and a governing board cut overhead for members who belonged to several projects, while each technical community kept its own steering committee and releases.

choices.choice: A lifecycle with a voting seat for graduates
choices.why: Tying a TAC vote to graduation gives mature, self-managing projects a say in the umbrella, while sandbox and incubating projects get more staff help instead.
A clear rule, 12 months without significant commits, keeps the project list honest about what is still maintained.
